title: NoSQL: choosing a model for the system requirements
lead: A product name cannot answer the essential questions: how fresh must the data be, how will the application access it, and how should the system handle failures?
goals: Explain the trade-off during a network partition.
Compare key-value, document, column-family, and graph data models.

sections.title: Separate two design decisions
sections.html:
A shop stores 300 GB of catalog and order data, and one machine is running out of capacity. There are two different ways to involve more machines. Divide the dataset into three 100 GB pieces, or copy the dataset to additional machines. The first creates room for different data; the second creates more places holding the same data.

Dividing logical rows is sharding or partitioning. Creating physical copies is replication. A system may do both: three 100 GB shards with two total copies of each require 3×100×2=600 GB for raw copies, before indexes, logs and other overhead. There are still 300 GB of logical records.

A known product key can route to its shard and an eligible replica. A query about every category may contact every shard. Copies can help reads and survive some failures, but writes must be propagated according to a policy. More machines do not remove communication or coordination.

Vertical scaling gives one machine more resources; horizontal scaling adds machines. Web applications motivated many NoSQL designs because traffic, data volume and update load grew quickly, while coordinating transactions across nodes was expensive. Restricting operations or accepting weaker freshness can simplify some distributed workloads. These choices have costs that the application must understand.

NoSQL, often expanded as “not only SQL,” names a family of approaches, not one guarantee. It does not mean all such systems lack transactions or all relational systems fail to scale. Flexible documents can have different fields, yet applications still need agreed types, units and validation. Choose the required behavior and access pattern before a product label.

Try it: if we double replica copies, does a logical COUNT(*) double?

No. Replicas are copies of the same logical data. They increase physical storage and propagation work, and may increase service capacity or fault tolerance. Correct query routing must not treat each replica as a new logical record.

Recall ACID from the transaction lessons: atomicity requires all operations or none; consistency means correct transactions preserve validity constraints; isolation controls concurrent interaction under the chosen guarantee; durability preserves committed effects through failures. JSON shape or a SQL/NoSQL label alone does not establish these properties.

sections.title: A network partition and a stale read
sections.html:
Replication introduces a question we cannot answer by choosing a data shape: what should a read return when copies cannot communicate? Follow this original history for one price, with no later writes.

TimeEastWestNetwork
0price=50price=50Connected
1RunningRunningLink fails
2Accepts price=60; acknowledges successStill price=50No propagation
3Write has completedNew read beginsStill partitioned

This communication split is a network partition; both servers may remain healthy. It is different from sharding, which deliberately places different data in different pieces.

If West returns 50, a read begun after the successful write sees an older value. That violates linearizability: operations should appear to use one copy while respecting real-time order. West cannot invent 60, because it has received no information about the write. If it waits for communication, an indefinitely long partition may prevent the read from completing. Rejecting the read also does not supply a valid read result.

CAP formalizes this conflict. C is linearizable read/write behavior; A requires requests at non-failing nodes eventually to complete with valid operation results. P allows communication partitions in the executions considered. A system cannot guarantee both C and A for every such execution. It is not a menu that freely chooses any two properties at all times.

The lecture's availability shorthand includes errors, which is too loose for the formal theorem. We use the primary Gilbert–Lynch definitions: an arbitrary refusal is not a successfully served read just because an error packet arrived. The guarantee concerns all permitted executions; it does not predict that every request in every partition fails.

CAP consistency concerns visibility and ordering. ACID consistency concerns preservation of application invariants by transactions. They share a word but ask different questions. Outside partitioned executions, CAP does not forbid providing both linearizability and availability.

Try it: West answers instantly with an error. Did the request become CAP-available?

No. A read requires a valid read result. A prompt rejection is a response in the everyday network sense, but does not satisfy this formal availability requirement. Keeping C by refusing some partitioned requests sacrifices that guarantee.

Key takeaway

CAP concerns the guarantees a system can provide when communication is disrupted by a partition. It is not a rule that lets a system freely choose any two of three properties at all times. CAP consistency also differs from ACID consistency, which concerns data invariants.

Sources and teaching scope

sections.title: BASE and application requirements
sections.html:
Suppose a profile change is acknowledged in East while West still holds the old profile. Later the connection works again and West receives the update. West's state changes even though no client wrote there. This is the intuition behind soft state: background propagation can change local state.

If updates stop and the required exchange/progress conditions hold, replicas eventually agree. That is eventual consistency. It does not specify how many seconds propagation takes or guarantee that the next read sees your last write. A delayed old read differs from losing an acknowledged committed update after a crash, which is a durability concern.

The acronym BASE groups Basically Available, Soft State and Eventual Consistency. “Basically available” expresses an aim to serve useful requests under chosen failure/consistency policies; the acronym is not proof every request succeeds under every failure. Soft state describes background change; eventual consistency describes convergence under its conditions.

Convergence alone does not decide conflicts. Imagine an initial cart {pen}. East adds book while West adds mug before exchanging updates. A merge policy retaining independent additions could produce {pen,book,mug}; a whole-cart last-writer policy could instead lose one addition. Both need precise semantics. Saying “eventual” does not select the policy.

Different application data tolerates different behavior. A view counter or recommendation may accept stated lag. Selling the same last seat twice violates inventory requirements. A system must enforce the reservation rule at the authoritative write path rather than hope replicas catch up quickly enough.

Try it: all replicas eventually show the same cart. Does that prove no addition was lost?

No. They may have converged on a policy that overwrote one concurrent addition. Agreement, freshness and preservation of intended updates are different requirements. Specify the merge policy and test the conflicting update history.

Key takeaway

Eventual consistency promises convergence under appropriate conditions. By itself, it does not promise immediate visibility of the latest write, a bound on convergence time, or a particular rule for merging concurrent updates.

sections.title: Four models and the questions they answer
sections.html:
Now return to the shop and change the question, one access pattern at a time. The data model should make the needed operation clear.

Retrieve a known session

A basic key-value API offers get(key), put(key,value), delete(key). For get('session:7'), the key names one item; its value is an opaque payload. A placement hash can route the key, and separate placement rules can put replicas in different failure domains. This differs from hashing inside one local table. Updates and read freshness still depend on the replication protocol.

“Find every user older than 25” does not name a key. The basic opaque-value API needs a scan, client processing or an added index/query mechanism. Real products may offer such extensions, so evaluate the actual API rather than extrapolate from the basic model.

Filter fields inside products

{"sku":"P7","tags":["blue","small"],"spec":{"weight":2}}

A document model exposes structured fields, including nested objects and arrays. Objects associate names with values; arrays are ordered sequences. ["a","b"] differs in order from ["b","a"]. For users An25, Bo26, Cy30, age>25 returns Bo,Cy; age≥25 also returns An. Types and boundary conditions still matter.

Flexible fields do not remove the need to define whether weight is numeric and measured in kilograms. Validation and transaction guarantees are separate from JSON shape. Relational systems can also store/query JSON; JSON is not exclusive to one family.

Read one device's recent measurements

A sparse column-family row keyed device:7 might contain time-named temperature cells 10:00=21 and 10:05=22. device:8 may contain only battery at 10:00=80. The second row need not store a temperature cell with NULL. The application must define what absence means. This access-oriented sparse-row organization differs from columnar OLAP storage that groups one attribute across many rows.

Fetching recent cells for one device follows its row key and cell names. Finding every device with temperature>25 may require another access design, index or broader scan; sparse storage is not a universal query shortcut.

Follow relationships

A property graph uses entity nodes, labeled directed relationships and properties on either. With An —FRIEND→ Bo —FRIEND→ Cy and An —DRIVES→ Car7, an exactly two-hop outgoing FRIEND pattern from An returns Cy. Car7 is not a friendship, and a direct edge alone does not satisfy two hops. Direction, label and path length define the question.

Try it: can one known-key lookup answer the age predicate over every profile?

No. Exact-key retrieval and field filtering are different access patterns. Similarly, a graph label does not make every outgoing edge a friend, and flexible JSON does not establish correct numeric types or multi-document atomicity.

Documents are not limited to JSON: Protobuf and XML are other structured-format examples in the slides. An interchange format, logical model and query API are related but distinct choices.

sections.title: Practice choosing a design
sections.html:
Choose a design by tracing the shop's operations. A catalog has changing product fields and queries on those fields. Checkout must reserve inventory atomically. Recommendations follow relationships and may tolerate a minute of lag. These requirements need separate answers even if one system ultimately serves all three.

  1. Catalog: define product identifiers, required fields, field types and indexes for actual filters. A document model can represent varying specifications, but missing units and unindexed filters remain problems.
  2. Checkout: make “reserve one if stock>0” an authoritative atomic operation or suitable transaction/protocol. Decide how failures and retries are handled. A cached number does not enforce the invariant.
  3. Recommendations: define the graph pattern and allowed freshness. A delayed recommendation can be acceptable without authorizing delayed inventory validation.

A single multi-model system or multiple synchronized systems can be reasonable. Multiple copies introduce propagation, operations and failure-recovery work. Evaluate those costs with the query path; merely naming three fashionable products is not a design argument.

Graph language names also need context. Cypher and GQL target property-graph querying; SQL/PGQ brings property-graph patterns into SQL; SPARQL queries RDF/semantic-web data. Models and syntax differ. A two-hop traversal and an aggregate across all nodes may favor different physical designs even in one graph system.

The lecture's popularity chart and March 2026 ranking are historical source snapshots. They are not current performance measurements or proof of transaction guarantees. The source lists Oracle first and MongoDB as Document, Multi-model; those labels do not answer our checkout question.

Try it: two buyers see one remaining item in a stale recommendation cache. How should checkout proceed?

Both must submit reservation requests to the authoritative inventory path. An atomic conditional update or correctly chosen transaction/protocol permits at most one to consume the remaining unit. The other receives the defined out-of-stock outcome. Choosing eventual recommendations does not require eventual inventory reservations.

Try it: should every outgoing edge from An count as a friendship recommendation?

No. Follow the FRIEND label, outgoing direction and required path length. DRIVES is a different relationship. A graph model stores relationships explicitly, but the query still determines which ones qualify.

Sources and teaching scope

The lecture's March 2026 table places Oracle first and labels MongoDB “Document, Multi-model”. These are facts about that source snapshot, not claims about today's ranking or an experimental performance result. Popularity signals cannot establish a system's latency, transaction semantics or fitness for one application. A product can support more than one data model.

quiz.question: Two replicas cannot communicate, and one has acknowledged a new write. What is the problem if a later read at the other replica immediately returns the old value?
options: It does not preserve linearizable consistency.
It cannot be a NoSQL system.
quiz.explanation: A read that starts after a successful write but returns the old value does not satisfy linearizability. This is the central trade-off illustrated by CAP.

source.summary: Lecture 27 covers the motivation for NoSQL, sharding and replication, CAP and BASE, data models, and workload-driven choices. This learning material also explains how to interpret simplified CAP diagrams carefully.
